doc.title: Dawoud Sabu Adeyola interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 30, 2025

title: Spirituality, Muslim musicians and music as more than music
summary: Musicians avoiding drugs through faith, Coltrane's quartet, meeting Yusef Lateef, and his memoir on music as connection and the blues.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: But you know I did a research project one time on Islam and bebop musicians but when I heard from a couple of those guys is that they used to all hang out in a certain mosque in Harlem. You know Monk, Rollins, even the ones who weren’t — a lot of them became Muslim outwardly and changed their names like Yusef Lateef, Ahmad Jamal you know, Sadik Hakin, the piano player. But then there were others people didn’t know like McCoy Tyner was Muslim, Art Blakey, Dakota Staton you know, Lynn Hope, the great

saxophone player. Even Kenny Clarke. Kenny Clarke when his book, his autobiography came out it had Kenny Clarke and then his Muslim name underneath it, I think it was Ali, something like that. And they tend to have a better grip on life. A lot of times they had families and they kind of avoided pitfalls. And so with me coming from a pretty much traditional home you know going to church at least once or twice a week, having ministers in the family and whatnot. All right? You know otherwise I could have been you know trying to turned to vice. I said no, no if you become a musician you’ve got to use drugs or you’ve got to be an alcoholic. That’s the norm. But there was this other group, you know that wasn’t about that you know. So that was — even when the John Coltrane Quartet came to the Royal Arms at Buffalo when I was in high school. And John at that time was — he was clean but his years of abuse had pretty much did his liver in and he only had a couple more years to live. But Jimmy Garrison and Elvin Jones, you know, were obviously intoxicated you know, and McCoy Tyner would just sit over by himself sipping on water or soda pop or something like that. And sometimes Yusef Lateef, when he came here, because I used to watch these guys. Yusef Lateef would come, sometimes he wouldn’t even leave the bandstand. On break they’d bring him coffee or whatever. He wouldn’t even leave the bandstand. He’d go, “I’m not even going down there.” So I said yeah, this is — I related to that. I met Yusef Lateef one time when I was a serviceman in Germany, I used to on my breaks sometimes I would just go to different cities and visit you know. And I went to Hamburg one time and Yusef was playing in Hamburg and I got a chance to sit and talk with him for a long time. And he told me about how you know his spirituality, how his religious, how his faith had kept him away from certain things that destroyed other musicians. And he actually gave me some books to read. So yeah, that was a big — it’s interesting you should ask because recently I saw an interview like this one, Alice Coltrane did an interview with Branford Marsalis. Have you seen that one?

Yeah, look it up. It’s online. It just came out I think. It’s really interesting when he asked her about it. And you know Alice is very spiritual you know, very much into the culture. And so was John of course, obviously, everybody knows. But I think Alice had some influence on him or it was probably mutual, that the music is more than just music. In fact in my memoir, which I hope to finish up hopefully by next year. I call it “It’s More Than Only Music” you know? More than only music you know. And that music is connections. Connection to the past. Musicians are like recorders you know, we’re like recorders or reporters of what’s going on in society, what’s going on at the time. And especially in the African-American experience, music was one of the few things that we were allowed to preserve something. Because we weren’t supposed to read or write or do

any of the literary things and so we do a careful analysis of the musical history whether it be blues, whether it be folk, or gospel or church music or whatnot, we can get a good idea of what was going on in terms of civil rights, in terms of human rights and human suffering and degradation. You can hear the cries in the music. And so that’s why I really think that the Lord Almighty gave us the blues, which seems it’s not going to ever go away you know and it has many forms. I mean almost all American music forms have some form of blues connection, whether it be jazz, country, rap, whatever they call it, the blues is just there you know.
You made me think of Joe Williams performed here and he introduced one song and he said, “Blues frees the spirit.”
